prompt: Each record sits in a retailer's customer database. Identify which kind of customer data it is.

cases.text: A shopper types her shoe size and favourite running brand into a 'Tell us about you' box so the app can suggest products.
cases.explanation: The consumer intentionally provided the details for a stated purpose: stated product preferences.

cases.text: In-store sensors log that a loyalty-card holder spent four minutes in the baby aisle last Tuesday.
cases.explanation: Dwell time and location are captured automatically from the consumer's interaction with the firm's physical property.

cases.text: A model assigns each account an estimated household income band from its purchases and postal code.
cases.explanation: The band is a probabilistic prediction generated by a model from volunteered and observed inputs.

cases.text: An analytics vendor collects 300,000 public forum posts about the retailer's products to train a sentiment model.
cases.explanation: The posts were harvested in bulk from public web pages without a direct relationship with the people who wrote them.

cases.text: Each subscriber's profile now shows a 'likely to cancel' score updated nightly.
cases.explanation: No subscriber supplied this. It is a prediction a model generates from their other data.

cases.text: A customer answers a post-purchase survey saying the delivery arrived late.
cases.explanation: Survey responses are intentionally provided by the consumer.

question_text: A fitness app shares each user's daily step counts with the user's chosen coach, as its sign-up page explains. The app then starts selling the same step counts to life insurers to price policies. Under contextual integrity, what makes the second flow a violation?
hint: Compare the two flows parameter by parameter: subject, sender, recipient, information type and transmission principle.
correct_answer_citation: Week 06: Contextual Integrity and Informational Norms

options.option_text: The step counts were secret, and any disclosure of secret data is a violation.
options.option_explanation: The data were already shared with the coach. Contextual integrity does not depend on whether the data were strictly secret.

options.option_text: The recipient changes from a chosen coach to insurers, and the transmission principle changes from coaching the user to commercial pricing, breaching the norms of the context.
options.option_explanation: Correct. The subject, sender and information type stay the same. Altering the recipient and the transmission principle breaches the norms under which the data first flowed.

options.option_text: Nothing is violated, because the information type (step counts) stays the same in both flows.
options.option_explanation: Changing any one of the five parameters can breach the norms, even when the information type is unchanged.

options.option_text: The violation is only that the user did not own the data and so could not sell it.
options.option_explanation: That is the property-ownership framing. Contextual integrity looks at whether the flow respects the context's norms.

prompt: Each design comes from a real-looking consent screen. Identify which dark pattern it uses.

cases.text: A photo editor will not open your pictures until you agree that your photos may be used to train its AI models.
cases.explanation: Basic functionality that does not need the data is made conditional on accepting AI training.

cases.text: The banner's 'Allow' button is large and bright. 'Decline' is pale grey text reading 'No, I prefer irrelevant ads'.
cases.explanation: The protective choice is styled in low contrast and framed with language that penalizes declining.

cases.text: After a quiet policy update, every existing account finds 'Use my messages to improve AI' already switched on.
cases.explanation: Accounts are enrolled automatically, exploiting status quo bias unless users notice and opt out.

cases.text: Turning AI training on is one tap on the home screen. Turning it off takes Settings, Privacy, Data, Advanced, then a confirmation page.
cases.explanation: Opting in takes one prominent click while opting out runs through nested settings menus: a roach motel.

cases.text: Joining a data-sharing programme takes one checkbox at checkout, but leaving it requires phoning customer service during office hours.
cases.explanation: The effort to opt out far exceeds the effort to opt in.

prompt: Sort each governance need into the safeguard from the slide that addresses it.

cards.text: A city publishes neighbourhood counts of welfare recipients and must guarantee that adding or removing any one household barely changes the published numbers.
cards.explanation: Differential privacy bounds how much one record can change the output distribution, by a factor epsilon.

cards.text: A phone keyboard should learn from what people type without their typed messages ever leaving the device.
cards.explanation: Federated learning trains on-device and sends only aggregated weight updates to the server.

cards.text: A former customer invokes the right to be forgotten and asks a bank to remove her records' influence from its trained credit model.
cards.explanation: Machine unlearning removes specific records' influence without retraining the whole model from scratch.

cards.text: A hospital trains a model with per-example gradient clipping and added noise so it cannot memorize any one patient.
cards.explanation: This is differentially private training (DP-SGD), with a governed privacy-utility trade-off.

cards.text: Five bank branches want a shared fraud model but may not pool raw transaction records in one place.
cards.explanation: Each site trains locally and shares only updates, ideally with secure aggregation.

cards.text: After a user deletes their account, a streaming service must show regulators that the user's history no longer shapes its recommendation model.
cards.explanation: Removing a specific individual's influence from an already trained model is machine unlearning.

prompt: Sort each proposed study into what an REB would decide under the rules on the slide.

cards.text: Participants are told a chatbot is a human travel agent, to test whether perceived humanity changes trust. The question cannot be studied otherwise, risk is everyday-level, and everyone is debriefed with the option to withdraw their data.
cards.explanation: Deception is necessary, risk is minimal, and debriefing with retroactive withdrawal is included.

cards.text: The same study as above, but to save time participants are never told the agent was a chatbot.
cards.explanation: Whenever deception is authorized, a debriefing with the right to withdraw is mandatory.

cards.text: Researchers want to tell participants a product review was written by a doctor when it was not, though disclosing the true author would answer the same question equally well.
cards.explanation: Deception is allowed only when the question cannot be answered without it.

cards.text: A firm calls households for a 'university consumer survey' whose last question asks for a credit-card number to buy the product.
cards.explanation: Commercial solicitation disguised as research (sugging) is strictly prohibited.

cards.text: Participants are falsely told an AI has flagged their real bank account for fraud, to measure stress responses, then debriefed.
cards.explanation: The harm exceeds what participants meet in everyday life, so the study is not minimal risk and deception cannot be authorized.

cards.text: Shoppers see prices labelled as set by 'a pricing expert' or 'an algorithm' in an online store mock-up. There is no other way to isolate the label, and all are debriefed.
cards.explanation: Incomplete disclosure about the source is necessary, low-risk and followed by debriefing.

question_text: A researcher has already collected interviews with twelve nurses from one small-town hospital. She now plans to delete each nurse's name and paste the transcripts into a public chatbot to code themes. What does REB oversight require first?
hint: Think about both what the consent form said and what remains in the text after the names are gone.
correct_answer_citation: Week 06: REB Oversight When AI Tools Process Participant Data

options.option_text: Nothing further: once names are removed the transcripts are anonymous.
options.option_explanation: Workplace descriptions, life events and verbatim quotes can still identify a nurse in a small hospital.

options.option_text: Only that she cite the chatbot in the methods section.
options.option_explanation: Citation does not address consent scope or third-party data transfer.

options.option_text: Only a distress protocol, because the chatbot might produce harmful outputs.
options.option_explanation: Distress safeguards matter for AI interviewers talking with participants. Here the issue is consent scope and identifiability.

options.option_text: The external AI processing and data transfer must have been disclosed in the consent form, and the text must be de-identified beyond names before any submission.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Third-party AI processing must be disclosed before participation, and stripping names alone does not make qualitative text anonymous.

prompt: Match each risk of replacing human panels with AI to the case that shows it.

pairs.match: Five hundred 'young urban renter' personas all rate a meal kit 6 out of 7, while real renters in a later survey spread from 1 to 7.
pairs.explanation: The simulated distribution is artificially tight and understates within-group heterogeneity.

pairs.match: Asked as a Kenyan farmer, the model describes weekend brunch and a suburban supermarket run.
pairs.explanation: The model fills gaps in an underrepresented persona with dominant Western norms.

pairs.term: Non-invariance to prompt and scale formatting
pairs.match: Rewording 'retired teacher' as 'senior on a pension' moves the panel's mean purchase intent by a full scale point.
pairs.explanation: A minor change in persona wording shifts the simulated sample's mean.

pairs.match: A transit agency reports that it 'consulted wheelchair users' on a new station design using only LLM personas.
pairs.explanation: Synthetic personas are used to claim consultation with a community whose real members were never asked or compensated.
